To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the expression of VCAM- 1 on endothelium of the central nervous system in mice with chronic graft-versus-host disease is significantly increased compared with that in syngeneic controls and that the absence of intercellular cellular adhesion molecule- 1 does not prevent leukocyte recruitment into brain parenchymal tissue in mice with chronic GvH D.

the expression of ICAM-2 and VCAM-1 was upregulated on cerebral endothel cells in mice with chronic GvH disease and that the cerebral endothelial expression of ICAM1 was not affected by ICAM1-deficiency.
the central nervous systems of mice with chronic graft-versus-host disease show upregulation of vascular cell adhesion molecular 1 on cerebral endothelial cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the central nervous system participates in graft-versus-host disease.
a new hypothesis of cerebral endothelial expression of adhesion molecules as an indicator for the occurrence of GvHD in the central nervous system.
a possible pathogenic link between GvHD and cerebral angiitis-like changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cerebral endothelium of mice with chronic GvHd expresses adhesion molecules in a pattern similar to that seen in the peripheral nervous system, but the cerebral endothelum does not seem to be involved in GvHd-associated brain parenchymal damage.
VCAM-1 is the adhesion molecule of the cerebral endothelium, which is upregulated during chronic GvHD and that this upregulation may play a role in the pathogenesis of GvHD.
the brain parenchymal damage in GvHD is not due to an inflammatory reaction but rather to the direct effect of the conditioning regimen on the central nervous system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the central nervous involvement in chronic GvHD does not result in cerebral histopathologic lesions and that the cerebral endothelium is involved in this process.
VCAM-1 is upregulated in cerebral endothelial cells of animals with chronic graft-versus-host disease and that this may play a role in the development of cerebral leukocytic infiltration.
VCAM-1 expression in cerebral endothelium of mice with chronic GvDH is a sensitive marker for the presence of leukocytic infiltrates in the central nervous system.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the central nervous systems of animals with chronic graft-versus-host disease do not appear to be damaged by infiltrating leukocytes, but that the cerebral endothelium expresses VCAM-1 as an adhesion molecule that may contribute to the pathogenesis of central nervous system involvement in chronic graft-versus host disease.
VCAM-1 is a key player in the pathogenesis of GvHD in the central nervous system.
VCAM-1 is a key mediator for recruitment of lymphocytes into the brain in chronic graft-versus-host disease, and it may be a potential target for treatment.
